title: Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols
keyIdea: Classify an alcohol by the carbon that carries the –OH group: if it is bonded to one other carbon the alcohol is primary (1°), to two it is secondary (2°), to three it is tertiary (3°). Warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI), primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids, secondary alcohols to ketones, and tertiary alcohols do not react, because their C–OH carbon has no hydrogen to lose. The orange dichromate turns green when an oxidation happens. Distil to collect the aldehyde; heat under reflux with excess oxidant to make the acid.

kid: Find the carbon that holds the –OH. Count the carbons joined to it. One means primary (1°). Two means secondary (2°). Three means tertiary (3°). The size of the whole molecule does not matter.

To oxidise an alcohol, warm it with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). The mix is orange. If the alcohol is oxidised, the dichromate turns green. Oxidation takes an H off the O and an H off the C–OH carbon. That leaves a C=O.

A primary alcohol gives an aldehyde first, with C=O at the end of the chain. Keep heating with more oxidant and it goes on to a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone, with C=O inside the chain. A tertiary alcohol has no H on its C–OH carbon, so it stays orange.

The kit decides where a primary alcohol stops. In distillation the aldehyde boils off as it forms, so you collect it. In reflux the vapour drips back into the flask, so the aldehyde is oxidised on to the acid.
adult: This is A-level organic chemistry (AQA 3.3.5 Alcohols, OCR A 4.2.1, Edexcel Topic 6). Students classify alcohols as primary, secondary or tertiary. They describe oxidation by acidified potassium dichromate(VI), with the colour change from orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ to green Cr³⁺. They write equations using [O] for the oxidising agent, for example CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CH₂CHO + H₂O and CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃CH₂COOH + H₂O.

The class depends on the carbinol carbon, the carbon bonded to –OH. A primary carbinol carbon carries two H atoms (methanol, with three, also counts as primary). A secondary one carries one H, and a tertiary one carries none. Oxidation removes the H from the O–H and one H from the carbinol carbon to form C=O. So a tertiary alcohol is not oxidised by dichromate, because a C–C bond would have to break. Propan-2-ol gives propanone: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O.

Conditions decide the product of a primary alcohol. Propanal boils at 48 °C, well below propan-1-ol at 97 °C and propanoic acid at 141 °C, because aldehyde molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other. If you distil as it forms, the aldehyde escapes. Under reflux with excess oxidant, it is oxidised to the acid. Tollens' reagent (silver mirror) or Fehling's solution (blue to brick-red) then tells an aldehyde from a ketone.

Common mistakes: classifying by the total number of carbons, or calling any branched alcohol tertiary (2-methylpropan-1-ol is primary). Expecting a secondary alcohol to go on to an acid. Saying the dichromate is oxidised; it is reduced. Forgetting the second [O] when an acid forms. In the lab students move an –OH round a branched skeleton, warm three alcohols with dichromate, build the C=O, and choose distillation or reflux.

familyTip: Draw butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol as skeletal formulae. For each one, circle the carbon holding the –OH, count its carbon neighbours, and write the class and the oxidation product next to it.

visual.caption: Primary, secondary or tertiary? Drag each alcohol, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: classify by the C–OH carbon's neighbours, warm alcohols with dichromate, build the C=O, and choose distillation or reflux.

practice.hint: Find the carbon with the –OH. How many carbons are bonded to it?
practice.explain: The C–OH carbon is bonded to two carbons (CH₃ and CH₂CH₃), so butan-2-ol is secondary. It oxidises to butanone.

practice.prompt: A primary alcohol with {n} carbons is heated under reflux with excess acidified dichromate. How many carbon atoms are in the carboxylic acid formed?
practice.hint: Oxidation changes the C–OH carbon into a COOH group. Does it add or remove carbons?
practice.explain: No C–C bond is made or broken, so the acid still has {n} carbons. Only the end CH₂OH becomes COOH.

practice.prompt: Which apparatus lets you collect ethanal from ethanol?
choices: Distil the ethanal off as it forms
Leave it at room temperature in a sealed flask
practice.hint: Ethanal boils at about 20 °C. What happens to it under reflux?
practice.explain: Distilling removes the ethanal as it forms, before it can be oxidised further. Reflux would turn it into ethanoic acid.

practice.prompt: In the equation for oxidising a primary alcohol all the way to a carboxylic acid, how many [O] are used for {n} moles of the alcohol?
practice.hint: Going to the aldehyde uses one [O]; going on to the acid uses a second.
practice.explain: Each mole needs 2[O], so {n} moles need 2 × {n} = {=2*n} [O]. RCH₂OH + 2[O] → RCOOH + H₂O.

pool.prompt: What is seen when propan-2-ol is warmed with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?
pool.hint: Propan-2-ol is secondary. Is a secondary alcohol oxidised?
pool.explain: Secondary alcohols are oxidised (to propanone here), so orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to green Cr³⁺.

pool.prompt: Why is 2-methylpropan-2-ol not oxidised by acidified dichromate?
choices: Its C–OH carbon has no H atom to lose
It has too many carbon atoms
pool.hint: Forming C=O needs an H to leave the C–OH carbon.
pool.explain: It is tertiary: the C–OH carbon is bonded to three carbons and no H, so C=O cannot form without breaking a C–C bond.

pool.hint: Ignore the branch. Look only at the carbon holding the –OH.
pool.explain: The –OH is on a CH₂ bonded to just one carbon, so it is primary even though the chain is branched.

pool.prompt: What is the organic product when butan-2-ol is heated under reflux with acidified dichromate?
pool.hint: Secondary alcohols give which kind of carbonyl compound?
pool.explain: A secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone, butanone, and goes no further under these conditions.

pool.prompt: What happens to the dichromate(VI) ion when an alcohol is oxidised?
pool.hint: The oxidising agent gains the electrons the alcohol loses.
pool.explain: The oxidising agent is reduced: Cr goes from +6 in Cr₂O₇²⁻ to +3 in green Cr³⁺.

pool.prompt: A primary alcohol with {n} carbons, CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH, is oxidised to the aldehyde by distilling. How many H atoms are in one aldehyde molecule?
pool.hint: Oxidation removes 2 H atoms: one from the O and one from the C–OH carbon.
pool.explain: The alcohol has 2 × {n} + 2 = {=2*n+2} H atoms. It loses 2, so the aldehyde has {=2*n} H atoms.

pool.prompt: {n} moles of a secondary alcohol are fully oxidised to the ketone. How many moles of water form?
pool.hint: R₂CHOH + [O] → R₂CO + H₂O. Read the ratio.
pool.explain: Each mole gives one H₂O, so {n} moles give {n} moles of water.

pool.prompt: Why does propanal distil off before it is oxidised further?
choices: It boils at 48 °C, below propan-1-ol at 97 °C
pool.hint: Aldehyde molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other.
pool.explain: Propanal has no O–H, so no hydrogen bonds between its molecules; it boils at 48 °C and leaves the hot mixture first.
